entities.name: Bardo National Museum
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Bardo National Museum (Musée National du Bardo), housed in the former Hafsid and Husainid palace complex outside Tunis — a 9th-century origin site expanded and rebuilt through Ottoman and then Husainid Bey eras — is the largest museum in North Africa and one of the world's greatest repositories of ancient Roman mosaic art, containing the most extensive and spectacular collection of Roman mosaics in existence, including room-sized masterpieces from Carthaginian and Roman North African sites.

The museum's Roman mosaic collection is extraordinary: hundreds of mosaics from the Roman provinces of Africa Proconsularis and Byzacena (modern Tunisia) represent the height of the art form — depicting mythological scenes, gladiatorial combats, marine life, portrait busts, and Dionysian revels in works that surpass anything found in Rome itself. The mosaics from the royal Bardo palace renovations and archaeological sites at El Djem (the third-largest Roman amphitheater), Thuburbo Majus, Dougga, and Utica provide unparalleled documentation of Roman provincial life in Africa.

Beyond the Roman collection, the Bardo holds Carthaginian steles and votives, prehistoric artifacts, Islamic arts, and the remarkable Mahdia shipwreck collection — a 1st-century BC Greek ship carrying Greek artworks looted for Roman buyers, salvaged in the 1900s. The museum suffered a devastating terrorist attack in March 2015, when Islamist gunmen killed 22 tourists and security guards — one of the worst attacks on cultural heritage in North Africa. This attack was both a tragedy for the museum and a statement of Islamist hostility to Western tourism and cross-cultural heritage.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Bardo National Museum — housing the world's greatest Roman mosaic collection, holding irreplaceable North African archaeological treasures, and surviving a 2015 terrorist attack that highlighted both its cultural significance and vulnerability — is Africa's most important ancient art museum and a vital window into the Roman world's African provinces.
